background_notes.fact: For real numbers u,v, |uv|=|u||v| and |u+v|<=|u|+|v|; iterating gives the analogous finite-sum bound. A nonzero integer has magnitude at least 1. Thus under L1 all sorted magnitudes and both products are positive, and each frequency magnitude is at most the sum of the other three.

grounds.reason: L1 states integer frequencies, nonzero product and zero sum; the magnitudes and products are explicitly defined there.

background_notes.justification: The absolute-value identities follow by the sign cases, and the triangle inequality follows by adding -|u|<=u<=|u| and -|v|<=v<=|v|. Integer nonvanishing gives magnitude >=1. Substituting each frequency as minus the other three and applying the finite triangle inequality gives the claimed comparison. All later divisions in these pointwise steps therefore have positive denominators.

background_notes.fact: For finitely supported real families u,v on an integer domain, |sum_k u(k)v(k)| <= (sum_k u(k)^2)^(1/2)(sum_k v(k)^2)^(1/2). For zero-extended shell restrictions and any integer s, sum_k u(k)v(s-k) <= ||u||_2||v||_2. Also, a nonnegative family supported on a set of cardinality M satisfies sum_k u(k)<=sqrt(M)||u||_2. The same correlation bound holds for shell-index families extended by zero at negative indices and any fixed integer shift.

grounds.reason: The inputs are first restricted to finitely many frequencies; two smaller frequencies are fixed, prescribing the sum s of the two larger ones. Each shell restriction has finite support.

background_notes.justification: For finite vectors, nonnegativity of sum_k(u(k)-t v(k))^2 and minimization in t proves Cauchy–Schwarz when the squared norm of v is positive; if it is zero then v=0. The map k->s-k is a bijection of the integers, so reflection and translation preserve the zero-extended squared norm. Applying the same inequality with the indicator of a finite support gives the sqrt(M) estimate. Shifts of zero-extended shell arrays preserve the full integer norm, and restriction to nonnegative indices cannot increase it.

background_notes.fact: The sets S_j={k in Z\{0}:2^j<=|k|<2^(j+1)}, j>=0, are a disjoint partition, with |S_j|=2^(j+1). For a finitely supported sequence x, defining X_j=(sum_{k in S_j}|x(k)|^2)^(1/2) gives sum_j X_j^2=sum_k |x(k)|^2. Restricting an ell^2 sequence to any subset cannot increase its norm.

grounds.reason: The domain is nonzero integers, shell indices are nonnegative integers, and Xshell is defined to be the shell ell^2 norm after finite restriction.

background_notes.justification: For each positive integer magnitude n, the increasing unbounded sequence 2^j brackets n uniquely; unboundedness follows, for example, from 2^j>=j+1. Each shell has 2^j positive and 2^j negative integers. The squared-norm identity for finite support is a finite disjoint regrouping. For arbitrary ell^2 sequences, all square terms are nonnegative, so every restricted square sum is bounded by the full square sum; taking square roots preserves the inequality.

background_notes.fact: For rho=2^(-1/2), 0<rho<1 and sum_{r>=0}rho^r=1/(1-rho). In particular every finite collection of the shell correlations in S004 is bounded by ||Xshell_3||_2||Xshell_4||_2/(1-rho).

grounds.reason: The shell difference r=ell-m is a nonnegative integer and each correlation is bounded by the same shell-norm product by the preceding Cauchy–Schwarz application.

background_notes.justification: The finite geometric sum equals (1-rho^(n+1))/(1-rho). The powers tend to zero: with h=rho^(-1)-1>0, Bernoulli's finite inequality gives rho^n<=(1+nh)^(-1), which tends to zero by the Archimedean property. Thus the supremum of these nonnegative partial sums is the displayed constant. Multiplying by the fixed nonnegative product bounds the correlations, uniformly in the supports.

background_notes.fact: Let t_i>=0 be indexed by I, and let finite sets I_m increase so that every finite F subset I is contained in some I_m. If sum_{i in I_m}t_i<=B for all m, with finite B, then the nonnegative sum sup_{F finite subset I}sum_{i in F}t_i exists and is <=B; it equals sup_m sum_{i in I_m}t_i. The same bound holds after restricting I to any subset.

background_notes.justification: Every finite subsum is bounded by a containing I_m subsum, using nonnegativity; conversely each I_m is itself a finite subset of I. These two comparisons identify the suprema. The family of finite subsums is nonempty (it includes the empty sum) and bounded above by B, so real completeness supplies its supremum. Subset finite sums form a subfamily and hence have no greater supremum. No interchange of conditionally convergent sums is needed.
